# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What it tells, in a few words | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | What its caption stands on |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **How the pieces stand:** a stack, a fan, a ring, a row, a wall, or what the chapter needs. The same pieces in every beat.
- **What is on their faces:** the person's real pictures and words. Name the picture.
- **What the chapter adds:** anything in the scene besides the pieces. Often nothing.
- **What its caption stands on:** a working title of a few words, and the lines of the fact sheet the caption will be written from. Not the caption.

**Write no captions yet.** The words are written at a later stop, where the person chooses them. A sentence written now, to make the script read well, is where a detail gets in that nobody told you: a hall that was "standing empty", a wheel that is "true again". So a beat names its facts and stops there. Where a beat wants something the fact sheet does not hold, such as what the work taught them or what was wrong before they came, put the question in its place.

## Someone with thirty seconds

Say how a visitor who does not scroll gets the name, what the person does, one proof of it, and how to reach them. The first screen carries the first three. A rail jumps to any chapter, and one link skips to the close.

## Without the scene

Say what a visitor gets in each case. The text is ordinary HTML over the scene, so all of it is there in every row. Say what stands in for the pieces.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | |
| With reduced motion | |
| With no WebGL | |
| With no JavaScript | |

## The look and the type

Both come from the object's material: plates are ceramic on linen, a status page is dark glass, a paper is white with dark ink. Name two or three looks, each as its ground, its ink, one accent, and the surface of the pieces. The person picks by scrolling, once it is built.

Two typefaces: one for the text, and one for what is printed on the pieces, which belongs to the form.

## Everything else the site needs

Mark every row build, later or never, and say who decided.

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | | |
| A page for each project | | |
| Every project listed | | |
| How to reach them, and a CV | | |
| What others say | | |
| Languages | | |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | | |
| The page for an address that is not there | | |
| A blog | | |
| A chat | | |
| A legal notice, where their country asks for one | | |

## What you ask for

A yes to the script, or what to change. Give the list of what you decided for them with it.

The full plan is saved in [storyboard.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-phd-with-yQ9fkq/docs/story/storyboard.md). **No website, prototype or assets have been built.**

The site follows one question: **What does it take to make a research result reproducible—and explain its limits?**

One 3D notebook, made of six shallow cell panels, stays with the visitor throughout. Its pieces rearrange to explain each chapter, then reunite at the end.

| Chapter | Content | Scroll behavior |
|---|---|---|
| **Research question** | Your name, doctoral-candidate role, contribution and under-review preprint | Six cells assemble into a notebook |
| **Inputs** | Public synthetic example and the restricted-data boundary | Public-example and boundary panels separate |
| **Workflow** | The reproducibility workflow you owned, supported by public code | Cells spread into ordered steps |
| **Sensitivity checks** | How results change when assumptions change | Cells fan into alternative paths |
| **Interpretation** | Association in one retrospective dataset; no demonstrated causation or clinical validation | Finding and limitation panels face the reader together |
| **Practical exercise / next steps** | Adapted exercises, two sections and 24 students; evidence and contact links | Cells open into an exercise layout, then reform the notebook |

The sequence takes roughly eight desktop screens. Movement follows normal scrolling and reverses smoothly when visitors scroll back. No camera tumbling or forced pauses. Sensitivity animation explains the method; numerical results appear only if verified public evidence supports them.

**Visual direction:** warm paper, charcoal ink, deep teal accents and matte notebook panels. Source Sans 3 carries the narrative; IBM Plex Mono carries code and cell labels. The plan also includes cool blue and dark notebook alternatives for later visual review.

**Immediate access:** the opening shows your identity, exact contribution and preprint status. Research, Code, CV and Email stay accessible without completing the story. Chapter links and a skip-to-close link support quick visits.

**Phones and accessibility:** phones use a single-column layout with static notebook illustrations by default. Reduced motion, unavailable WebGL and disabled JavaScript all retain the complete text, evidence links and navigation. Essential information remains ordinary HTML.

**Future implementation:** static or prerendered content, with a progressively loaded Three.js scene using simple geometry. The plan includes sharing metadata, a notebook icon, a missing-page screen and checks for factual accuracy, attribution, accessibility and performance.

Before implementation, we need the public repository and preprint URLs, licences and credits, CV destination and final email address. Any additional screenshots or figures need established display permission. Final captions remain for editorial review; the storyboard records their supported facts.

The decisions made for you are listed in [decided-for-you.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-phd-with-yQ9fkq/docs/story/decided-for-you.md).

**Do you approve this storyboard, or want any changes?** Approval accepts the plan only.

The [storyfolio skill](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-phd-with-yQ9fkq/.agents/skills/storyfolio/SKILL.md) requires “A yes to the script, or what to change” at this final planning stop. Your instruction against building remains in force.
